source_refs.note: Book p. 183-184: 6.3.1 derivation of y^2 = 4ax with Figure 6.11.

blocks.text: Let \(F\) be the focus and \(CD\), the directrix of the parabola. Draw \(FZ\) perpendicular from the focus \(F\) to the directrix \(CD\). Let \(V\) be the mid-point of \(FZ\) and let \(FZ = 2a\). Take \(V\) as the origin, the \(x\)-axis along the line \(ZF\) and \(y\)-axis along the perpendicular to \(VF\) at \(V\), as shown in the figure.

blocks.alt: On a pale yellow panel, the parabola y^2 = 4ax (cyan) with vertex V at the origin of magenta axes X'X and Y'Y (arrows at both ends), focus F(a, 0), and the cyan directrix CD (arrows at both ends) crossing the axis at Z; a point P(x, y) on the parabola is joined to F and to the foot M of its perpendicular on the directrix.
blocks.caption: Figure 6.11: Focus F, directrix CD and a point P of the parabola (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 6.11)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Why these axes? We are free to put the axes anywhere; we choose them so that the equation becomes as short as possible. With \(V\) at the origin and the \(x\)-axis through the focus, the focus is \((a, 0)\) and the directrix is the vertical line \(x = -a\). Here \(a > 0\) is the distance from the vertex to the focus (and also from the vertex to the directrix).
Since \(V\) is equidistant from the focus and the directrix, by definition, the point \(V\) lies on the parabola. The point \(V\) is called the vertex of the parabola.
Thus, the focus of the parabola is \(F(a, 0)\) and the directrix is \(x = -a\).

Let \(P(x, y)\) be any point on the parabola and draw \(PM\) perpendicular to \(CD\). Therefore,
\[|PF| = \sqrt{(x-a)^{2} + (y-0)^{2}}\]
\[= \sqrt{x^{2} - 2ax + a^{2} + y^{2}}\]
Distance of \(P\) from the directrix \(x = -a\) is
\[|PM| = \dfrac{|x + a|}{\sqrt{1^{2} + 0^{2}}} = |x + a|\]

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Two distance formulas are used here.
\(|PF|\): the distance formula between two points \((x, y)\) and \((a, 0)\).
\(|PM|\): the distance from a point to a line. Write the directrix as \(x + a = 0\), i.e. \(1\cdot x + 0\cdot y + a = 0\); then the distance is \(\frac{|x + a|}{\sqrt{1^{2} + 0^{2}}}\). Since \(M\) has the same \(y\) as \(P\), this is simply the horizontal gap between \(x\) and \(-a\).

By the definition of a parabola, \(|PF| = |PM|\). Therefore,
\[\sqrt{x^{2} - 2ax + a^{2} + y^{2}} = |x + a|\]
Squaring both sides, we get
\[x^{2} - 2ax + a^{2} + y^{2} = (x + a)^{2}\]
\[x^{2} - 2ax + a^{2} + y^{2} = x^{2} + 2ax + a^{2}\]
which simplifies to
This is the standard equation of the parabola.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
The simplification the book leaves out: cancel \(x^{2}\) and \(a^{2}\) from both sides:
\[-2ax + y^{2} = 2ax\]
\[y^{2} = 4ax\]
Why is squaring safe here? Both sides are distances, so both are \(\ge 0\); for non-negative numbers \(p = q\) exactly when \(p^{2} = q^{2}\). Also \(|x + a|^{2} = (x + a)^{2}\), so the modulus disappears.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Reading the equation \(y^{2} = 4ax\) (with \(a > 0\)):
Since \(y^{2} \ge 0\), we need \(x \ge 0\): the whole curve lies to the right of the \(y\)-axis, i.e. it opens towards the focus, away from the directrix.
Replacing \(y\) by \(-y\) does not change the equation, so the curve is symmetric about the \(x\)-axis.
For example, with \(a = 1\) the curve \(y^{2} = 4x\) passes through \((0, 0)\), \((1, \pm 2)\), \((4, \pm 4)\).

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Choice of axes: vertex at the origin, \(x\)-axis through the focus.
2. Then focus \(F(a, 0)\), directrix \(x = -a\), vertex \(V(0, 0)\), and \(a\) = distance vertex to focus.
3. Standard equation: \(y^{2} = 4ax\).
4. Derivation in one line: \(|PF| = |PM|\), square, cancel.
5. The curve opens to the right and is symmetric about the \(x\)-axis.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Taking \(a\) as the distance from focus to directrix. That distance is \(2a\); \(a\) is half of it.
2. Writing \(|PM| = x - a\). The directrix is \(x = -a\), so \(|PM| = |x - (-a)| = |x + a|\).
3. Expanding \((x + a)^{2}\) as \(x^{2} + a^{2}\) and losing the middle term \(2ax\).
